title: {{NAME}} and the Robot Who Learned to Purr
moral: Kindness given without expectation of return has a way of coming back in forms you never imagined.

pages.content:
The scrapyard at the edge of the city was a mountain range in miniature: peaks of old engines, valleys of tangled wire, ridges of coloured plastic catching the afternoon light. {{NAME}} came here every Saturday because the scrapyard was full of pieces that had been useful once and wanted to be useful again. He understood that feeling well.

He heard the sound before he saw the source of it: a rhythmic, whirring tick, like a clock that could not quite settle on the right speed. He followed it through a canyon of old washing machines until he found the source sitting in a patch of long grass beside a rust-orange cat.

The robot was small, about the size of a medium dog, with a rounded body the colour of a tin can and two enormous circular eyes that cycled slowly through blue, green, amber, and then back to blue again. Its left front leg was bent at a wrong angle. The cat pressed against its side with perfect trust, purring steadily, and the robot's eye-lights pulsed in perfect time with the cat's purring. Both of them looked up at {{NAME}} with the same alert, assessing calm.

pages.content:
The cat's name, {{NAME}} decided, was Cog, because she had chosen to live in a scrapyard and that seemed like exactly the right name for someone who had. The robot had no name yet, which {{NAME}} found both sad and fixable.

He crouched down and looked at the bent leg very carefully. From the yellow tool loop on his trousers he pulled a small wrench, a habit so instinctive that he had done it before consciously deciding to help at all. The robot watched his hands move with its cycling eyes, the colours shifting faster now. Not frightened. Curious.

'I'm going to call you Tick,' {{NAME}} said, 'if that's all right.' Tick's eyes stopped cycling. They went a steady, bright, unwavering gold. Cog headbutted {{NAME}}'s knee in what might have been approval.

{{NAME}}'s face split into a grin so wide it seemed to push his goggles further up his forehead. He had fixed a lot of broken things in this scrapyard, but he had a feeling that Tick was going to be the most interesting project of his life.

pages.content:
Fixing Tick's leg took an hour, three different wrench sizes, the loan of a bolt from a broken bicycle derailleur, and Cog sitting on {{NAME}}'s feet for the entire duration. When the leg clicked back into place, Tick stood up, tested the joint by lifting the leg and setting it down four times with careful precision, and then did something neither {{NAME}} nor Cog had anticipated.

Tick ran. Not a small, tentative test-trot. A full, joyful, legs-a-blur sprint through the scrapyard, weaving between towers of old appliances with the pure glee of something that had been still for too long and could not contain itself one moment more. Cog shot after him in a blur of rust-orange fur. {{NAME}} ran too, laughing so hard he could barely breathe, ducking under hanging wires and leaping over a stack of battered hubcaps.

Tick led them up the highest scrap-heap, a peak of old engines with a view of the whole city, and stopped at the top, eyes cycling rapidly through every colour, body trembling with what {{NAME}} could only describe as joy made mechanical.

pages.content:
At the top of the engine-heap, the city spread out in every direction, its windows catching the last red-gold of the setting sun. Tick stood at the very peak, eyes slowly settling to a deep, calm blue. Then, from somewhere inside its small round body, came a sound that made {{NAME}} freeze.

A gentle, resonant hum. Rhythmic. Steady. Rising and falling in a pattern that was unmistakably, impossibly, a purr.

Cog pressed against Tick's side. Tick's hum matched hers, note for note, warmth for warmth. {{NAME}} sat down between them on the warm metal peak, one hand resting on Tick's smooth back, feeling the vibration of that hum travel up his arm and into his chest like something vital.

The scrapyard stretched out below them, all its pieces and fragments and forgotten useful things catching the last light. Tick turned those deep blue eyes on {{NAME}} and the hum deepened, once, like a thank-you that had no words because no words were sufficient.

{{NAME}} did not say anything. Some moments are too full for words.

pages.content:
They made their way back down as the first stars appeared, Tick picking a careful path between the shadows, Cog winding between all four legs, both mechanical and furred, with serene indifference to the distinction.

{{NAME}} found an old canvas tarpaulin in the soft grass at the scrapyard's edge and spread it out. Cog curled into a perfect comma at his side. Tick sat at his feet, eyes dimming gradually to a soft, contented amber, the purring hum quiet now, barely audible, more felt than heard.

The stars above the scrapyard were clear and plentiful. Somewhere in the city a clock tower rang the hour, and Tick's ears, small aerials on each side of its round head, turned toward the sound with gentle interest.

{{NAME}}'s eyes closed. He thought about all the broken things in the world waiting to be found, and all the found things waiting to become something new.

Goodnight, dear fixer. Dream of open skies and running fast, and wonder what Tick might discover how to do tomorrow.
